Compare Norwegian Nynorsk flatbrødsoll (“flatbrød in milk”).

52489.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse skankr (“leg, shank”), from a Proto-Germanic ablauting noun represented by Proto-Germanic *skankô (“that which is bent; shank, thigh”), with related stem variants *skinkan- and *skunkan-. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keng- (“to limp, hobble; to tilt, be askew”), probably through the semantic development “crooked, bent” → “leg, shank”.
Related to skinke (“ham”), borrowed from a Middle Low German descendant of the related Proto-Germanic variant *skinkô (“thigh, shank”), and sjenkel (“lower leg; rider's leg”), borrowed from German Schenkel, a diminutive formati

en.g: E-sharp; the note E raised by a semitone, enharmonically equivalent to F, or the written note denoting this pitch
x: I denne akkorden må e spilles som eiss.
In this chord, E must be played as E-sharp.
Derfor blir kryss for e (eiss) akkurat det samme som f, og kryss for h (hiss) akkurat det samme som c.
Therefore, E with a sharp (E-sharp) is exactly the same as F, and H with a sharp (B-sharp) is exactly the same as C.

1004041.etyen:
From e (“E”) + -iss (“sharp-note-forming suffix”). The suffix is from German -is (“sharp-note-forming suffix”); its further origin is uncertain.
Compare the parallel formations Swedish eiss, Danish eis, German Eis, Icelandic eís and Finnish eis (“E-sharp”).

PIE word

Ivar Aasen noted in 1878 that Botolv was commonly pronounced with open o in both syllables and was therefore often written Bottolf.
The underlying name ultimately continues Old Norse Bótólfr, a variant of Bótulfr. The Old Norse name is formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and úlfr (“wolf”), literally “remedy-wolf”. The first element is from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed- (“to improve, make better”). The second element is from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz (“wolf”), ultimately from Proto-In
